extracted.intended_audience: observational astronomers / natural philosophers / Royal Society readers interested in aurora observations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conclusions for recording and interpreting visual observations of the aurora borealis, including geometric relations to the magnetic meridian, height estimates, temporal behaviour, and recommended corroboration by multiple observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arch orientation relative to magnetic meridian
rubrics_metrics.description: The arch of the aurora, when at the zenith, is placed at right angles to the magnetic meridian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verified by many observers and cited repeatedly; treat perpendicularity to magnetic meridian as a primary geometric property to record and test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zenith arch narrowness (breadth at zenith)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the zenith the arch is only of small breadth (previously stated maximum ~5°; commonly 3°–5°; occasionally about 6° or more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report breadth in degrees at zenith; note that narrowness at zenith is a reproducible feature though occasional broader values occur (author revises earlier maxima based on later observations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction of streamers toward a point south of the zenith
rubrics_metrics.description: Streamers are directed to a point apparently a little south of the zenith; earlier estimate 10°–15° south, revised to about 15° (±3°–4°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record angular displacement of streamer convergence point from the zenith; allow for observational uncertainty of a few degrees and note that extremely evanescent features limit precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamers parallel to magnetic meridian / plane of dip
rubrics_metrics.description: The streamers, in the direction of their length, coincide with the plane of the dip of the needle, or nearly so; each individual streamer is parallel to the dipping needle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record local magnetic variation/dip and compare streamer alignment; this magnetic relation is fundamental and repeatedly corroborated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fringe-like arrangement: thin E–W fringe at right angles to magnetic meridian
rubrics_metrics.description: They form a thin fringe, stretching often a great way from E. to W. at right angles to the magnetic meridian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the aurora as a fringe/zone across azimuth, noting extent E–W and relation to magnetic meridian; useful for explaining brightness differences due to line-of-sight integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent southward motion via extinction/formation of streamers
rubrics_metrics.description: The fringe moves away from the N. magnetic pole by the extinction of streamers at its northern face, and the formation of new ones contiguous to its southern face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting motion, note changes in northern vs southern streamers (extinction vs formation) rather than assuming bulk translation; time and sequence of streamer birth/death are diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple parallel arches/fringes can be contemporaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be several nearly vertical fringes or parallel arches almost contemporaneously within the field of view; different observers at different places may thus report seemingly inconsistent positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and look for multiple parallel structures; when reconciling reports from multiple locations, consider multiple distinct fringes rather than a single high arch passing between sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aurora often contiguous to and interacting with clouds (low altitude implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of auroral light apparently touching, illuminating, or terminating abruptly at cloud edges indicate the aurora occupies a region immediately above and contiguous to that in which aqueous vapour is forming (cloud layer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record relationships to visible clouds (apparent contact, abrupt termination over cloud edges, illumination of cloud undersides), because these are key evidence towards low altitude of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Height estimates: likely low (thousands of feet) not extremely high
rubrics_metrics.description: The aurora's region is argued to be only a few thousand feet above the surface in many cases (lower ends perhaps ~2,000 ft; upper parts a few thousand feet more), contrasting with claims of ~100 miles altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cloud interactions, perspective effects, and horizon brightness to constrain height; document circumstances (moonlight, intervening hills, observed contact with clouds) that justify low-altitude inferences and note atmospheric variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brightness near horizon argues against very great altitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The frequent brilliance of light at the horizon would be difficult to reconcile with an origin one hundred miles high because of atmospheric obscuration; this supports a much lower altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When auroral brightness near horizon is observed, record it as evidence against very high-altitude models; include consideration of refraction and atmospheric path length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of breadth and streamer behaviour with elevation
rubrics_metrics.description: As an arch rises toward and passes the zenith it often becomes diminished in breadth and better defined; after passing beyond zenith it may again increase in breadth and renew short streamers at the vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record temporal evolution of breadth and streamer formation as the arch changes elevation; these systematic changes are diagnostic of the phenomenon's geometry and dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamer geometry: angle changes with distance from vertex
rubrics_metrics.description: At the vertex streamers are short, compact, and parallel to the magnetic meridian; towards the extremities streamers increase in length and form more acute angles with the arch's general line, approaching parallelism near the extremities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note streamer lengths and angles relative to arch line and magnetic meridian at multiple points (vertex vs extremities); these spatial patterns should be documented in degrees where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luminous intensity distribution can vary (extremities vs zenith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reports state the light towards the extremities to be more intense than at the zenith, while others report nearly uniform brightness throughout; both occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document intensity distribution across the arch (uniform, stronger at extremities, stronger at vertex) and note observer position and line-of-sight effects that may explain differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational parameters to record (angles, timing, motion speed, context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record azimuth/elevations (degrees from horizon/zenith), breadth in degrees, exact times, apparent motion (e.g., moved ~40° in ~10 minutes), terminations at horizons/clouds, concurrent moonlight, and wind/cloud conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide quantitative angular and temporal measures whenever possible and contextual meteorological data (wind direction, cloud heights, barometer/thermometer readings if available) to support height and dynamical inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with westerly/south-westerly gales and seasonal timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The aurora is most frequent at the period of the westerly equinoctial gales and often precedes or accompanies westerly and south-westerly winds; in winter it appears immediately before or during a westerly fresh wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record concurrent wind direction and seasonal timing; correct for historical misprints (author notes a misprint of 'south-easterly' in prior work) and prefer westerly/south-westerly association in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of multi-observer verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of an individual's natural phenomena should be fully verified by others; contemporaneous reports across locations are used to test and refine inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage coordinated observations across sites and times; compare elevations, timings, and appearance notes to resolve apparent discrepancies and to test hypotheses about number, height, and motion of arches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent irregularities off-zenith are often optical illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The invariable regularity of appearance when the aurora is near the zenith shows apparent irregularities seen when it is more northerly or southerly to be only optical illusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret highly irregular appearances seen off-zenith cautiously; seek zenith observations or corroboration to distinguish true structural irregularity from perspective/optical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-of-sight integration explains brightness differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A line from the eye directed considerably towards the East or West would penetrate and collect the light of many parallel streamers, making extremities appear more intense than a line directed near the zenith which penetrates fewer streamers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concept of line-of-sight integration to explain differences in observed intensity with viewing direction; when reporting brightness, note observer azimuth relative to fringe orientation.
